rationale: A Washington grand jury's refusal to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, the key Jan. 6 committee witness, was the day's top US national story (9 US outlets, 7 front pages) and another setback in the Justice Department's prosecutions of Trump critics. Focal. The NPR midterm poll ranked second but is a forecast that is hard to draw truthfully; Israel's election (no clear winner in exit polls) is international with no result yet; Bolsonaro's reported move to the US and the D.C. golf course ruling were smaller. No Boston story matched the national significance. One story keeps the picture clear.

stories.name: Grand jury declines to indict Cassidy Hutchinson
facts: A federal grand jury in Washington declined the Justice Department's request to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, a former aide to Trump chief of staff Mark Meadows, according to people familiar with the proceedings.
A Justice Department lawyer told a magistrate judge at an unrelated hearing on Tuesday that a grand jury had not concurred on a proposed indictment; sources said the defendant was Hutchinson.
Hutchinson was a star witness at the House Jan. 6 committee's 2022 hearings; Republican lawmakers had accused her of lying under oath. The exact charges sought were not made public.
Neither Hutchinson nor the Justice Department commented publicly in the first reports.

people.name: Cassidy Hutchinson

stories.visual_notes: Grand jurors are private individuals: anonymous, generic, seated. The unsigned indictment is the focal object. Hutchinson appears only in a halftone panel of her 2022 televised testimony (shoulder-length blonde hair, seated at a witness table with a microphone). Don't draw Trump, a courtroom verdict, Hutchinson reacting today, any vote count, or readable text.
stories.confidence: high: reported independently by AP (two sources), CBS (four sources) and NBC, plus a DOJ lawyer's statement in open court; the indictment was not made public, so details of the charges are not shown.
